What do the probe and the meter actually say to each other?

Fig 5 · The conversation

    The letter in the light gate (or being checked) right now, spot by spot. A hole lets light through = 0; paper stays dark = 1. Start spot, 7 letter spots (smallest first), a parity spot that makes the dark spots between the brackets an even number, and a stop spot.

    Meter colour

    The big idea: every letter is ten flashes in a row, and both sides must count them at the same speed.

    Where the numbers come from
    • The whole conversation (sign-on /?! at 300 baud, the meter's name with its speed letter 5, the acknowledgement ␆050, the 200 ms wait, then the data at 9600 baud ending in a BCC) and every letter on both tapes come from figure 1's model, so the two figures agree. Protocol as summarised in the OpenMUC j62056 guide and the Elseta IEC 62056-21 manual.
    • Times: 10 spots per letter (start, 7 data, even parity, stop). The 64-letter readout is 640 spots: 640 ÷ 300 = 2.133 s, 640 ÷ 9600 = 0.067 s, 32× faster. The whole conversation takes 1.433 s of real time; the stopwatch's red mark is where it would end if the readout stayed at 300 baud.
    • The checksum: XOR of every byte after STX up to and including ETX (IEC 62056-21, per OpenMUC). XOR is adding without carrying, so each wheel just flips when a letter has a 1 in its place. Here it comes out 0x7E, the letter ~.
    • Even parity, 7 data bits, 1 stop bit at 300 baud: the settings reader drivers use, e.g. the Mervis IEC 62056-21 driver. One flipped bit always makes the count odd, so parity catches any single flip; two flips in one letter would slip past it, which is why the BCC is there too.
    • After a failed check the phone “asks again”: reader software retries on a communication error (the Mervis driver's retry count). The standard's own rule for a bad BCC in readout mode is not checked here.
    • The tape machines are a picture of the light link, not real hardware: the probe has no paper. Light on = 0 and dark = 1, as in figure 1 (how DIY read heads wire it; check the standard's optical clause before relying on it). The meter's name, serial and total are invented, as in figure 1.
